note: One entry per clip. 'segments' is the narration: one line per on-screen caption, in the order the captions appear in the scene.

segments.caption: Start with an ECG recording that has no label.
segments.text: We start with a single lead ECG recording, ten seconds long. Nobody has labeled it with a diagnosis, so all we have is the raw signal.

segments.caption: Cut the signal into one-second patches: each patch becomes a token.
segments.text: We cut the signal into one second patches. Just like words in a sentence, each patch becomes one token for a transformer encoder.

segments.caption: Hide most of the patches at random.
segments.text: Then we hide most of the patches at random. Here, six of the ten patches are masked out.

segments.caption: The encoder sees only the visible patches.
segments.text: The encoder sees only the four visible patches, and turns each of them into an embedding vector.

segments.caption: A small decoder predicts the missing waveform from the encoder's output.
segments.text: A small decoder takes these embeddings, plus a placeholder mask token for every hidden patch, and predicts the missing waveform.

segments.caption: The loss compares prediction and truth only on the hidden patches.
segments.text: The loss is the mean squared error between the prediction and the true signal, computed only on the patches that were hidden.

segments.caption: To fill the gaps, the encoder has to learn what a heartbeat looks like.
segments.text: Over many training steps, the predictions improve. To fill the gaps well, the encoder has to learn the structure of a heartbeat: the P wave, the Q R S complex, and the T wave.

segments.caption: After pretraining, keep the encoder and discard the decoder.
segments.text: After pretraining, the decoder has done its job and is discarded. We keep the encoder, which now produces useful representations of ECG signals.

segments.caption: The same recipe works for pathology: hide image patches, reconstruct the pixels.
segments.text: The same recipe works for pathology. A masked autoencoder hides most patches of an H and E tile, here twelve of sixteen, and learns to reconstruct the missing pixels.

segments.caption: Make two augmented views of the same ECG.
segments.text: Contrastive learning starts by making two different views of the same ECG, using random augmentations.

segments.caption: Augmentations change the recording, not the diagnosis.
segments.text: Here, view one is cropped and has added noise, and view two is rescaled with a slow baseline drift. The heart rhythm, and so the diagnosis, stays the same.

segments.caption: One shared encoder maps each view to a point in embedding space.
segments.text: Both views pass through the same encoder, with shared weights. Each view becomes one point in the embedding space.

segments.caption: The other ECGs in the batch add more points.
segments.text: In practice we train on a batch, so the other ECGs in the batch, here B, C, and D, also become points.

segments.caption: Training pulls the two views together and pushes the other ECGs apart.
segments.text: Training pulls the two views of ECG A toward each other, and pushes the other ECGs in the batch further away.

segments.caption: The loss asks: which view in the batch is my partner?
segments.text: The loss turns this into a classification. Compare A one with every other view in the batch, apply a softmax, and its partner, A two, should win, here with zero point five nine.

segments.caption: This is the InfoNCE loss: a softmax over similarities with temperature τ.
segments.text: This is the info N C E loss. It is a softmax over the similarities, each divided by a temperature tau, and we minimize the negative log probability of the true partner.

segments.caption: Without any labels, similar ECGs tend to end up close together.
segments.text: After training on many unlabeled ECGs, recordings with similar rhythms tend to land close together, even though the model never saw a single diagnosis.

segments.caption: For pathology tiles, views come from crops, flips, and stain color changes.
segments.text: For pathology tiles, the two views come from random crops, flips and rotations, and changes in stain color, because tissue has no fixed orientation and staining varies between labs.

segments.caption: Take the pretrained encoder and freeze its weights.
segments.text: Now we test what pretraining learned. Take the pretrained encoder and freeze it, so none of its weights can change.

segments.caption: Now use a small labeled set: atrial fibrillation versus normal sinus rhythm.
segments.text: We need only a small labeled dataset. Here, each ECG is labeled either atrial fibrillation, A F, or normal sinus rhythm.

segments.caption: The frozen encoder turns each ECG into a 256-dimensional embedding.
segments.text: The frozen encoder maps each ECG to an embedding of two hundred fifty-six numbers. We draw these embeddings as points in two dimensions.

segments.caption: Add one linear prediction head: a weighted sum of the embedding plus a bias.
segments.text: On top, we add a single linear prediction head. It computes a weighted sum of the embedding plus a bias, and a sigmoid turns that into the probability of A F.

segments.caption: Training updates only the head; the encoder gets no gradient.
segments.text: During training, gradients flow into the head only. The encoder is frozen, so its weights never change.

segments.caption: If one line separates the classes, the information is already in the embedding.
segments.text: If one straight line can separate A F from normal, the information was already in the embedding. The head only has to read it out.

segments.caption: Fine-tuning updates the encoder too, so a probe is the cleaner test of pretraining.
segments.text: With fine-tuning, every weight is trainable, including the encoder. A linear probe trains only two hundred fifty-seven weights, so it measures what the pretrained encoder already learned.

segments.caption: The same probe works for pathology: tumor versus normal mucosa.
segments.text: The same linear probe works for pathology. A frozen encoder embeds each H and E tile, and a single linear head separates tumor from normal mucosa.
